cards.front: Recall a key point about Globalisation and Legislation
cards.back: Globalisation is the increasing interconnection of world economies through trade, investment, and technology - it means businesses can operate internationally more easily.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Globalisation and Legislation
cards.back: Multinational corporations (MNCs) operate in multiple countries: they benefit from lower labour costs and new markets but face cultural differences and complex regulations.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Globalisation and Legislation
cards.back: Employment law protects workers: National Minimum Wage, Working Time Regulations, Health and Safety at Work Act, Equality Act (preventing discrimination).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Globalisation and Legislation
cards.back: Consumer protection legislation (Consumer Rights Act 2015) ensures products are as described, fit for purpose, and of satisfactory quality - giving consumers the right to refunds, repairs, or replacements.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Globalisation and Legislation
cards.back: Legislation creates compliance costs for businesses (training, monitoring, documentation) but also sets minimum standards that protect stakeholders and create a level playing field.

cards.front: What should you know about business exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating legislation, use the PEST framework: Political (government policy direction), Economic (compliance costs vs productivity gains), Social (worker and consumer protection), Technological (how laws adapt to new tech). Always conclude by weighing protection benefits against compliance costs.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Globalisation only benefits large multinational corporations. Correct: Globalisation also benefits small businesses through: access to international markets via e-commerce, cheaper imported raw materials, technology that enables remote work and global collaboration, and cultural diversity that inspires new products.
